name: Greater Israel
summary: Greater Israel (Eretz Yisrael HaShlema, the whole Land of Israel) is the position that the Jewish people hold a permanent national, and for religious adherents divinely given, right to the entire land between the Mediterranean and the Jordan, and in older Revisionist versions east of the Jordan too. Its adherents oppose partition, territorial concessions and a Palestinian state west of the Jordan, and treat Jewish settlement and Israeli sovereignty throughout the territory as a central national task. Secular Revisionists argue from national right and security behind an 'iron wall' of Jewish force, while religious Zionists in the tradition of the Kooks see holding and settling the land as part of redemption.
scope: Two strands that share the territorial core: (1) the secular Revisionist line of Ze'ev Jabotinsky, Herut and the Likud as reflected in the Iron Wall essay, the Revisionist and Herut programmes, the 1977 Likud platform and Begin's 1977 autonomy plan; and (2) the religious-settler line of Abraham Isaac Kook and Zvi Yehuda Kook, Gush Emunim, Tehiya and today's Religious Zionist party, including Bezalel Smotrich's 2017 'Decisive Plan' (read through a scholarly analysis that quotes it at length). Where these strands split (democracy versus divine command, the status of Arab residents, religion in public life, social questions) the answer is 0 or low confidence. It excludes the maximal Nile-to-Euphrates reading, the Kach movement's explicit transfer programme and the 1967 Labor-movement supporters of the Movement for Greater Israel, whose socialist economics differ. Economic answers follow the documented Revisionist/Herut positions and are mostly low or medium.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Herut, the main Revisionist party, paired its criticism of heavy state intervention with a call for a national health insurance system; the religious-settler strand has no distinct position.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Revisionists favoured private initiative and private capital, and Herut called itself a liberal party that would block socialism; today's Religious Zionist party also generally backs free markets.

state-harmful.rationale: Zvi Yehuda Kook told his students that the State of Israel is the state the prophets foresaw, a stage of redemption, and Revisionism's aim was a sovereign Jewish state; both strands treat the state as sacred or essential.

empower-police-military.rationale: The Iron Wall doctrine makes armed force the precondition of settlement, and later platforms pledge to destroy armed Palestinian organisations, so adherents favour strong security forces.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: The Religious Zionist alliance has opposed recognising same-sex marriage, while secular Likud adherents vary; strands are split.

abortion-legal.rationale: Religious settlers lean against abortion while the secular Revisionist tradition is silent; strands are split.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The NZO aimed to revive the Jewish state and language and implant Jewish tradition, and the Religious Zionist party campaigns on strengthening the state's Jewish character.

nation-first.rationale: Platforms put the Jewish people's eternal right to the land above outside peace proposals and reject externally designed solutions.

open-borders.rationale: The doctrine is about fixing and holding national borders at the Jordan, and settler programmes reject any second national movement west of it, which is incompatible with open borders.

revolution-justified.rationale: Begin's Irgun, from the Revisionist camp, waged armed revolt against British rule, though Jabotinsky preferred legal pressure; strands and periods are split.

central-planning.rationale: Revisionists favoured private capital with minimal state involvement and Herut pledged to block any attempt to establish socialism.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Herut defined itself as a liberal party opposed to socialism and Revisionists favoured private capital, which rules out abolishing money and wages.

democracy-best.rationale: Jabotinsky and Herut worked through parliamentary means, but Gush Emunim holds that the land may not be surrendered even by an elected government; strands are split.

right-to-secede.rationale: The doctrine's core is that no part of the land west of the Jordan may be handed to any foreign administration, which excludes a region's right to secede.

political-violence-never.rationale: Jabotinsky argued that settlement must proceed behind an iron wall of force, and the Revisionist Irgun fought an armed struggle against British rule.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Gush Emunim prefers Jewish law to democratic decision on the land, while the secular Revisionist strand does not; strands are split.

military-superiority.rationale: The Iron Wall essay says settlement can only continue under a force the native population cannot break through, so Jewish military dominance is the doctrine's precondition.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The Revisionist aim was a Jewish majority on both sides of the Jordan, and Jabotinsky pictured a Jewish-majority state with an Arab minority.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Revisionists rejected class conflict during state-building, proposing to outlaw strikes and lockouts and arbitrate disputes nationally.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: The doctrine treats the Jewish people as the land's rightful owners by eternal right and opposes handing any of it to the Arab population's administration.

direct-action.rationale: Nulled: the statement now asks whether direct action should replace electoral politics (reworded 2026-11-10, Codex review). This answer rested on direct action used alongside elections or on a mixed record, which does not support agreeing that it should replace them; its sources need re-reading against the new text.

reviewHistory.rationale: Gush Emunim set up settlements ahead of government approval to create facts on the ground, while Jabotinsky and Herut preferred parliamentary methods; strands are split.

collective-farming.rationale: Revisionists criticised collective agricultural settlement as draining capital from the private economy and favoured small private plots.

national-rebirth.rationale: The NZO aimed at the redemption of the Jewish people and the revival of its state and language, and Tehiya ("Revival") took its name from that idea.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: The 1977 Likud platform declares the Jewish people's right to the Land of Israel eternal and inseparable, and the Revisionist aim was a Jewish state with a Jewish majority.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: The Likud platform pledges to encourage diaspora Jews to come and settle the land, and Revisionist economic planning was built around mass Jewish immigration.

revive-national-language.rationale: The NZO's stated aims included the revival of the Jewish people's state and language.

national-self-determination.rationale: Read as a universal principle, adherents reject it: platforms oppose any Palestinian state west of the Jordan and Smotrich holds there is no room in the land for a second national movement.

force-without-un.rationale: The doctrine rejects outside-imposed solutions and relies on Israeli force rather than international approval to secure the land.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The religious strand grounds the land claim in faith and redemption, while Jabotinsky argued from morality and reason; strands are split, leaning toward disagreement.

class-collaboration.rationale: Revisionists rejected class struggle during state-building and proposed compulsory national arbitration between employers and workers.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Religious strands hold traditional gender views while secular Revisionists do not legislate them; strands are split.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Jabotinsky pledged equal rights for Arabs, while Smotrich's plan offers Palestinians residency without citizenship; strands are split, leaning toward formal agreement.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Adherents present Jewish settlement as realising an eternal right to the homeland and pledge not to dispossess anyone; Jabotinsky used the word colonisation but held it moral and just.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Jabotinsky wrote that Zionist colonisation must proceed regardless of the native population because its consent will not come, and Gush Emunim places holding the land above any democratic decision.

population-transfer.rationale: Jabotinsky said he would never eject anyone and the Likud platform pledges not to dispossess, while Smotrich's plan encourages emigration of Palestinians who keep national aims; strands are split.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The Revisionist programme proposed outlawing strikes and lockouts during the period of state-building in favour of compulsory arbitration.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The doctrine centres on undiminished Jewish sovereignty from the sea to the Jordan, which is incompatible with pooling sovereignty in a supranational union.

minority-language-support.rationale: Jabotinsky's Helsingfors programme gave minorities cultural rights, while the settler right stresses the state's Jewish character; strands are split.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: The Likud platform rejects handing any part of western Eretz Israel to foreign rule, Tehiya opposed any territorial concession, and Kook asked whether Jews had the right to give up even a grain of the land.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: The doctrine holds that Israel's sovereignty between the sea and the Jordan is a right, not an occupation, and later programmes call for formally imposing sovereignty on all of Judea and Samaria.

refugee-return.rationale: Begin's autonomy plan let Arab refugees into the territories only in a reasonable volume agreed unanimously with Israel, and the doctrine's aim of a Jewish majority excludes a general right of return.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Jabotinsky offered the Arab minority national-cultural rights on the Helsingfors model, but Herut spoke only of civic equality and Smotrich wants municipal bodies without national character; strands are split.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The doctrine rests on Jewish immigration and settlement in the homeland; Jabotinsky framed Zionism as the claim of a homeless people to land of its own.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Today's religious-Zionist programme would curb High Court review and let the Knesset reinstate struck-down laws, but Jabotinsky's liberal legalism points the other way; strands are split.

patriotic-education.rationale: The Religious Zionist party campaigns for strengthening Jewish education and national identity, and the Revisionist Betar movement schooled youth in national loyalty.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The modern settler right seeks to limit judicial review of Knesset laws, while Jabotinsky backed civil liberties; strands are split, leaning against entrenchment today.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Gush Emunim holds that even an elected government may not give up the land, which some read as licence to resist withdrawal, while Revisionists were legalist; strands are split.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Both strands demand active political engagement: Jabotinsky built mass movements and Gush Emunim mobilised settlers to shape state policy.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: The doctrine reserves sovereignty over the land to the Jewish people and opposes any Palestinian national entity west of the Jordan.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Revisionists were legalist, though Gush Emunim placed divine command above government decisions on the land; strands are split.

national-law-over-international.rationale: The Likud platform rejects externally imposed solutions, and the doctrine holds Israel's sovereignty over the land regardless of international rulings.

religious-nation.rationale: For religious Zionists the nation and its land are bound by divine covenant, while Revisionists defined the nation in secular national terms; strands are split, leaning toward agreement.

religion-illusion.rationale: The religious strand holds the return to the land is the fulfilment of prophecy and redemption, and even Revisionism aimed to implant Jewish tradition in national life.

majority-settlement.rationale: The Likud platform calls settlement across the land the core of Zionism, and Smotrich's plan calls for moving hundreds of thousands of Israelis into Judea and Samaria to create irreversible facts.

historical-land-claim.rationale: The Likud platform calls the Jewish right to the Land of Israel eternal, Kook taught that the land is bound to the Jewish people by a living bond, and Gush Emunim treats it as divinely allotted.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Herut's fierce opposition to the 1952 reparations agreement with West Germany rested on memory of the Holocaust, which the movement treats as historical fact.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Not applicable; the doctrine opposes armed Palestinian resistance.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Gush Emunim places divine command over democratic decisions on the land, while Revisionists ground authority in the nation; strands are split.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Jabotinsky's Iron Wall essay holds that settlement can only proceed behind a force independent of the native population.

racial-franchise.rationale: Within Israel adherents accept Arab citizens' vote, but Smotrich's plan denies territorial Palestinians citizenship and national voting; strands are split.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Secular Likud adherents accept it while religious-settler parties oppose LGBT recognition; strands are split.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Religious Zionists want strengthened Jewish education and the NZO aimed to implant Jewish tradition in national life, so promoting atheism runs against both strands.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The doctrine reserves sovereignty to the Jewish people and Smotrich rejects any room for a second national movement, so executive power-sharing with Palestinians is excluded.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Betar, the Revisionist mass youth movement, organised young people for national service and self-defence.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Jabotinsky's doctrine treats armed self-defence as the basis of Jewish survival in the land.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: The doctrine's eternal right rests on an unbroken bond between the Jewish people and the land, which Kook describes as essential to the nation's very being.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The religious strand frames politics as redemption, while the secular strand does not; strands are split.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Revisionists sought a Jewish majority through mass immigration and the Likud platform encourages diaspora Jews to settle, so the homeland is meant to gather the people, not only inspire them.

culture-before-state.rationale: Jabotinsky wrote that it did not matter whether the Jewish state would be orthodox or socialist so long as a state existed, putting statehood first.

person-over-state.rationale: Jabotinsky's individualism affirms it while the religious strand treats the land and nation as above individual choice; strands are split.

sacred-nation.rationale: Kook held that the land and nation share a holiness beyond rational explanation, and Revisionism called for the redemption of the Jewish people.

premarital-sex.rationale: Religious adherents disapprove while secular Revisionists are silent; strands are split.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Religious settlers hold the Torah's promise of the land literally while secular Revisionists do not; strands are split.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Begin's 1977 plan offered Arab residents administrative autonomy, while Gush Emunim rejected autonomy and Smotrich allows only municipal bodies; strands are split.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Gush Emunim holds that the land's retention is divinely ordained and cannot be overturned by human or democratic decision, and the Likud platform rejects any transfer to foreign rule.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: The doctrine's central task is Jewish settlement throughout Judea and Samaria, especially in Arab-populated highlands, so it rejects limits on settlement in majority-Arab areas.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Kook's Orot describes the Land of Israel as bound to the Jewish nation's soul, not an external possession, and Gush Emunim treats protecting it as a religious duty.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Strands split: religious settlers of Gush Emunim placed divine command above state decisions on the land, while secular Revisionists and Likud stressed state law.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Herut combined national loyalty with an appeal to workers and national health insurance and free schooling, treating national and social aims as compatible.

material-over-identity.rationale: The doctrine puts national and, for the religious strand, religious identity and territory above economic interests; the position is itself an identity politics.

police-more-powers.rationale: The Iron Wall doctrine makes armed force the precondition of settlement, and later platforms pledge to destroy armed Palestinian organisations, so adherents favour strong security forces. (Moved from empower-police-military, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about military spending alone.)

missingStatements.text: A state should apply its full sovereignty to territory it controls and claims as part of its homeland, rather than leave it under military administration or negotiate its future status.
missingStatements.rationale: Asserting sovereignty over Judea and Samaria is the doctrine's programme, from the 1977 Likud platform to Tehiya's annexation demand and Smotrich's call to impose sovereignty on all of it.
missingStatements.declined: Statement bank frozen on 2026-10-22, before the people audits: no new statements are added.

notes: Strands that would answer differently: Jabotinsky's own liberal minority-rights programme (equal citizenship, national-cultural autonomy) versus Smotrich's residency-without-citizenship and encouraged emigration; Revisionist parliamentary legalism versus Gush Emunim's view that the land cannot be surrendered even by an elected government. The 1967 Movement for Greater Israel also drew Labor-movement figures (Tabenkin, Alterman) with socialist economics, excluded here. Two sources (s15, s17) are critical commentary and s6 is a Palestinian research centre's analysis; they are used for what they quote or report, not their framing.
